sentences.text: Mandrasuchus is the oldest confirmed alligatorine, appearing within the first million years after the K-Pg event.
It reached about two metres in length, slightly smaller than the 2.3-metre Borealosuchus specimens from Corral Bluffs.
Some evidence hints that Mandrasuchus may have engaged in burrowing behavior.
The holotype — the specimen on which the species is based — is catalogued as DMNH EPV.48541 and preserves a skull, tail, osteoderms, and limb fragments.
The specific epithet milleri honors Ian Miller, who uncovered many specimens at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science.
Mandrasuchus was likely a macro-generalist predator, capable of tackling large prey and crushing the shells of molluscs, crustaceans, and turtles.
Its heterodont dentition — teeth of differing shapes — supports a versatile diet comparable to that of modern alligators.
Mandrasuchus belongs to the extinct genus of alligatorines.
Phylogenetic analyses place it within the subfamily Alligatorinae.
Lessner and colleagues prefer a topology that treats Navajosuchus specimens as separate and unconstrained.
Mandrasuchus lived during the Danian stage of the Paleocene.
Its type locality is the Denver Formation.
Fossils have been recovered from the United States, specifically Colorado.
The species’ fossil range is confined to the Early Paleocene (Danian).
There is ongoing debate about whether teeth and osteoderms found near the K-Pg boundary in Weld County belong to Mandrasuchus, because similar dentition occurs in Late Cretaceous crocodilians.
